parent_reference.heading: 1. At a Glance
parent_reference.content:
- **Topic**: Check
- **Difficulty**: Beginner
- **Typical age**: 6+
- **Estimated teaching time**: 20 min
- **Piece/concept type**: Rule
- **Prerequisites**: TOP-104 King Movement

**🎯 Today's Goal:**
Your child will recognize when their King is under attack and successfully use all three methods (Run, Block, Capture) to save the King.

**✅ Lesson Success Criteria:**
- The child identifies when a King is in Check.
- The child knows they cannot ignore a Check.
- The child can demonstrate Running, Blocking, and Capturing to escape Check.

*(Purpose: "Can I teach this today?" A quick summary for busy parents.)*

parent_reference.heading: 2. Definition
parent_reference.content: "Check" is the chess term for when a King is directly attacked by an enemy piece. Because the King can never be captured, the game has a strict rule: If your King is in Check, you MUST get out of Check on your very next turn. You cannot choose to ignore it, and you cannot make any move that does not save the King. There are exactly three ways to get out of Check: **Run** (move the King to a safe square), **Block** (put one of your pieces in between the King and the attacker), or **Capture** (take the attacking piece off the board).

parent_reference.heading: 3. Why It Matters
parent_reference.content: This is the core mechanic of chess. If a child does not understand Check, they cannot play a legal game. More importantly, learning the three ways to escape Check (Run, Block, Capture) forces the child to look at the *entire board* to find creative solutions, rather than just panicking and moving the King.

parent_reference.heading: 4. Before You Teach (Graph)
parent_reference.content:
- **Requires:** TOP-104 (King Movement)
- **Unlocks:** TOP-020 (Checkmate), TOP-022 (Castling)

parent_reference.heading: 5. Parent Understands
parent_reference.content:
Check is simply a threat to capture the King on the next turn. However, because the King is immortal, the threat must be resolved. 
If a player accidentally ignores a Check and moves a different piece, that move is **illegal**. You must force them to take their move back and fix the Check. 
It is common courtesy (but not an official rule) for beginners to say the word "Check!" out loud when they attack the enemy King.

parent_reference.heading: 6. How to Teach It
parent_reference.content:
1. **The Fire Alarm:** Place the White King in the center. Place a Black Rook far away on the same file. Tell your child, "The Rook's laser is pointing right at the King! The King is in CHECK. When you hear the word Check, a loud fire alarm goes off: WEE-OO-WEE-OO! You have to stop everything and put out the fire!"
2. **Method 1: RUN:** Ask the child, "Can the King run out of the laser?" Have them step the King one square to the side to a safe file. 
3. **Method 2: BLOCK:** Put the King back in the laser. Give the child a White Pawn. Ask, "Can you build a wall to block the laser?" Have them place the pawn between the Rook and the King. "The fire alarm stopped!"
4. **Method 3: CAPTURE:** Put the King back in the laser. Remove the pawn. Give the child a White Knight and place it near the Black Rook. Ask, "Can you smash the fire alarm?" Have the Knight jump over and capture the Rook. 
5. **The Golden Rule:** Emphasize that if you are in Check, you CANNOT do anything else until the King is safe.

parent_reference.heading: 7. Teaching Story / Analogy / Memory Hint
parent_reference.content:
**The Three Ways to Survive a Snowball Attack:**
Imagine someone is throwing a snowball at the King! (CHECK!) What can the King do?
1. **RUN!** Step out of the way so the snowball misses.
2. **BLOCK!** Hold up a shield (another piece) so the shield gets hit instead.
3. **CAPTURE!** Have a bodyguard tackle the guy throwing the snowball!

parent_reference.heading: 8. Did You Know? 🎓
parent_reference.content: In the official rules of tournament chess, you actually do not have to say the word "Check" out loud! It is the other player's responsibility to notice the fire alarm going off on the board. But for kids, saying "Check" is a fun and helpful tradition.

parent_reference.heading: 9. Board Diagram 1 — Basic Concept
parent_reference.content:
![DGM-019-01: A Black Rook aiming a red arrow straight down the file at the White King.](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-019/DGM-019-01.svg)
*The King is in Check! The fire alarm is ringing!*

parent_reference.heading: 10. How It Works
parent_reference.content:
When you are in Check, your brain should automatically go down the checklist:
1. Can I **Capture** the bad guy? (Usually the best option).
2. Can I **Block** the bad guy? (Good if the attacker is far away).
3. Do I have to **Run**? (The last resort).

parent_reference.heading: 11. Board Diagram 2 — Practical Example
parent_reference.content:
![DGM-019-02: White is in check from a Black Bishop. A White Knight is shown capturing the Bishop to solve the check.](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-019/DGM-019-02.svg)
*Method 1: CAPTURE the attacker.*

parent_reference.heading: 12. Real Game Example
parent_reference.content:
![DGM-019-03: White is in check from a Black Queen. A White Pawn moves forward to block the path.](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-019/DGM-019-03.svg)
*Method 2: BLOCK the attack by putting a piece in the way.*

parent_reference.heading: 13. Common Mistakes
parent_reference.content:
- **Ignoring the Check:** A child gets so focused on attacking their opponent's pieces that they completely ignore the fact that their own King is in Check.
- **Always Running:** Beginners panic when in Check and immediately move their King, completely forgetting to check if they can just capture the attacker for free!
- **Blocking a Knight:** You cannot "Block" a Knight's check, because Knights jump over walls! You can only Run or Capture.

> **🧑‍🏫 Coach Tip:**
> When your child is in Check, do not let them touch the King immediately. Make them sit on their hands and say out loud: "Can I capture it? Can I block it?" before they are allowed to run.

parent_reference.heading: 14. Teaching Notes
parent_reference.content:
This is a critical moment in their chess development. If you don't drill the "Run, Block, Capture" checklist now, they will develop a permanent bad habit of running their King around the board in a panic. 

> **🧑‍🏫 Coach Tip:**
> Use the letters **A.B.C.** to remember the escapes (but slightly modified!): 
> **A**void (Run)
> **B**lock
> **C**apture

parent_reference.heading: 15. Parent FAQ
parent_reference.content:
**Q: What if the King can't run, can't block, and can't capture?**
A: Then the fire alarm never stops... and the game is over! That is called Checkmate. We will learn that in the very next lesson!

**Q: Can I put my own King into Check on purpose?**
A: No! The rules of chess forbid you from ever making a move that puts your own King into danger.

parent_reference.heading: 16. Practice Together
parent_reference.content:
**The Firefighter Drill:**
Set up a White King in the middle of the board, surrounded by a few White helpers (a Knight, a Bishop, a Pawn). You hold a Black Queen. 
Slam the Black Queen down somewhere to put the King in Check and yell "FIRE ALARM!" 
The child has 10 seconds to find a way to save the King (Run, Block, or Capture). Once they save him, you pick up the Queen, move her somewhere else, and yell "FIRE ALARM!" again. Do this 5 times fast.

parent_reference.heading: 17. Coach Challenge ⭐
parent_reference.content:
**The Best Escape:**
Set up a board where the White King is in Check from a Black Rook. 
Make sure it is possible for White to Run safely, to Block with a Pawn, AND to Capture the Rook with a Knight. 
Tell your child: "You have three ways out of this burning building. Which one is the BEST way?" 
Help them realize that **Capturing** the Rook is the best choice because it eliminates a dangerous enemy piece for free!

parent_reference.heading: 18. Try It Yourself
parent_reference.content:
### 🟢 Recognition (Easy)
![DGM-019-04: White King on g1. Black Bishop on d4 aiming at g1. White Pawn on f2 blocking the path.](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-019/DGM-019-04.svg)
**Question:** The Black Bishop is looking at the White King. Is the White King in Check?
**Answer:** No! The White Pawn on f2 is already acting as a shield, blocking the laser. The fire alarm is NOT ringing.

### 🟡 Application (Medium)
![DGM-019-05: White King on e4. Black Knight on d6 (Checking the King). White Bishop on b8 (can capture Knight).](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-019/DGM-019-05.svg)
**Question:** The White King is in Check by the horse! Can you block the horse? 
**Answer:** No! You can never block a Knight because it jumps over things! You must either Run away with the King, or Capture the Knight using the White Bishop on b8.

### 🔴 Challenge (Hard)
![DGM-019-06: White King on h1 in check by Black Queen on h5. White has a Rook on c5.](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-019/DGM-019-06.svg)
**Question:** The White King is trapped in the corner and cannot Run! He cannot Capture the Queen. What is the only way to save him?
**Answer:** You must Block! The White Rook on c5 can slide over to h5 (Wait, c5 to h5 is horizontal, it lands between the Queen and King). Let's say Rook slides to h5 to block the Queen! (Note: The Rook moves to h5 to stand in the way of the Queen's attack down the h-file).

parent_reference.heading: 19. Continue Learning
parent_reference.content: - **Lichess Practice:** [Check](https://lichess.org/learn#/10) (Interactive drills to escape check).

parent_reference.heading: 20. Related Topics
parent_reference.content:
- **Prerequisites:** TOP-104 King Movement
- **Next Steps:** TOP-020 Checkmate, TOP-022 Castling

parent_reference.heading: 21. Parent Confidence Check ✅
parent_reference.content:
- [ ] Do I understand what Check means?
- [ ] Do I know the rule that you MUST escape Check?
- [ ] Can my child name the 3 ways out of Check (Run, Block, Capture)?
- [ ] Did we practice the "Firefighter Drill"?

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.text:
- **Topic**: Check
- **Difficulty**: Beginner
- **Typical age**: 6+
- **Estimated teaching time**: 20 min
- **Piece/concept type**: Rule
- **Prerequisites**: TOP-104 King Movement

**🎯 Today's Goal:**
Your child will recognize when their King is under attack and successfully use all three methods (Run, Block, Capture) to save the King.

**✅ Lesson Success Criteria:**
- The child identifies when a King is in Check.
- The child knows they cannot ignore a Check.
- The child can demonstrate Running, Blocking, and Capturing to escape Check.

*(Purpose: "Can I teach this today?" A quick summary for busy parents.)*

sections.title: Definition
sections.text: "Check" is the chess term for when a King is directly attacked by an enemy piece. Because the King can never be captured, the game has a strict rule: If your King is in Check, you MUST get out of Check on your very next turn. You cannot choose to ignore it, and you cannot make any move that does not save the King. There are exactly three ways to get out of Check: **Run** (move the King to a safe square), **Block** (put one of your pieces in between the King and the attacker), or **Capture** (take the attacking piece off the board).

sections.title: Why It Matters
sections.text: This is the core mechanic of chess. If a child does not understand Check, they cannot play a legal game. More importantly, learning the three ways to escape Check (Run, Block, Capture) forces the child to look at the *entire board* to find creative solutions, rather than just panicking and moving the King.

sections.title: Before You Teach (Graph)
sections.text:
- **Requires:** TOP-104 (King Movement)
- **Unlocks:** TOP-020 (Checkmate), TOP-022 (Castling)

sections.title: Parent Understands
sections.text:
Check is simply a threat to capture the King on the next turn. However, because the King is immortal, the threat must be resolved. 
If a player accidentally ignores a Check and moves a different piece, that move is **illegal**. You must force them to take their move back and fix the Check. 
It is common courtesy (but not an official rule) for beginners to say the word "Check!" out loud when they attack the enemy King.

sections.title: How to Teach It
sections.text:
1. **The Fire Alarm:** Place the White King in the center. Place a Black Rook far away on the same file. Tell your child, "The Rook's laser is pointing right at the King! The King is in CHECK. When you hear the word Check, a loud fire alarm goes off: WEE-OO-WEE-OO! You have to stop everything and put out the fire!"
2. **Method 1: RUN:** Ask the child, "Can the King run out of the laser?" Have them step the King one square to the side to a safe file. 
3. **Method 2: BLOCK:** Put the King back in the laser. Give the child a White Pawn. Ask, "Can you build a wall to block the laser?" Have them place the pawn between the Rook and the King. "The fire alarm stopped!"
4. **Method 3: CAPTURE:** Put the King back in the laser. Remove the pawn. Give the child a White Knight and place it near the Black Rook. Ask, "Can you smash the fire alarm?" Have the Knight jump over and capture the Rook. 
5. **The Golden Rule:** Emphasize that if you are in Check, you CANNOT do anything else until the King is safe.

sections.title: Teaching Story / Analogy / Memory Hint
sections.text:
**The Three Ways to Survive a Snowball Attack:**
Imagine someone is throwing a snowball at the King! (CHECK!) What can the King do?
1. **RUN!** Step out of the way so the snowball misses.
2. **BLOCK!** Hold up a shield (another piece) so the shield gets hit instead.
3. **CAPTURE!** Have a bodyguard tackle the guy throwing the snowball!

sections.title: Did You Know? 🎓
sections.text: In the official rules of tournament chess, you actually do not have to say the word "Check" out loud! It is the other player's responsibility to notice the fire alarm going off on the board. But for kids, saying "Check" is a fun and helpful tradition.
